destination.title: Police Can Force Your Thumb — But Maybe Not Your Mind

short31: An officer at your window wants your phone open.
But your mind may be the one lock he can't force.
Your phone isn't a phone — it's your whole life.
In 2014, Riley versus California said police generally need a warrant to search it.
But a warrant is worthless if they can't get in — so the real fight is whether they can force you to open it.
That jumps to the Fifth Amendment, which shields the contents of your mind.
A passcode lives in your head, so many courts say it may be protected.
But your face and thumb are on your body — no thought required — and the law often treats them like a booking fingerprint.
So in 2024, one federal court let officers press a man's own thumb to unlock.
A year later, another called almost the same act unconstitutional.
States split on passcodes too — and the Supreme Court has refused to settle it.
Your right can change at a state line.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: There has never been a record of a human being this complete.
Your phone has sat in rooms no one else was in.
No human being alive knows you the way that glowing rectangle does — and it never forgets a single thing.
In 2014, in a case called Riley versus California, the justices ruled — unanimously — that a phone is not like anything else you carry.
So the real fight was never really about searching.
None of that is testimony — it reveals nothing you know.
Which leads somewhere most people never see coming.
In 2024, a federal appeals court — the Ninth Circuit — looked at a case where officers took a man's phone and simply pressed his own thumb to the sensor to unlock it.
For years the government has claimed it can search your phone there with no warrant at all — and the courts cannot agree on how far that power goes.
In 2023, one federal judge became the first to rule that the government does need a warrant to search a phone at the border — a real crack in the wall.
But that too is unsettled, and it binds almost no one yet.
It has never decided whether you can be forced to unlock your phone at all.
But your mind — the passcode you never say out loud — may be the last thing they can't force.
We never quite decided what happens when someone else holds them up to the lock.
Until we do — until a court finally says where the line is — the only key they may never be able to take from you is the one you never speak.

lines.text: Everything the courts are fighting over about your phone gets thinner in one place. The border.

lines.text: At an airport, or a crossing, the normal rules bend. For years the government has claimed it can search your phone there with no warrant at all.

lines.text: Inside the country the rule looks settled. Riley versus California, 2014: police generally need a warrant to search a phone.
source_lines: In 2014, in a case called Riley versus California, the justices ruled — unanimously — that a phone is not like anything else you carry.
Before the police can search what's inside it, even after an arrest, they generally need a warrant.

lines.text: A phone holds every place you have been and every message you have sent, down to the minute.
source_lines: Every place you've been, mapped by the minute.
Every message you've sent, every photo you've taken, who you love, what you fear, what you searched at three in the morning.

lines.text: But one judge is not a national rule. There is no national rule, only a patchwork of courthouses.
source_lines: So there is no national rule.
decided not by what they did, but by which courthouse happened to be looking at them.

shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If a flicker of choice is what the Fifth Amendment protects, where does that leave the face scan you set up for convenience?

lines.text: A federal court let officers press a man's own thumb to his phone. Then it added a line that undoes almost everything.
source_lines: In 2024, a federal appeals court — the Ninth Circuit — looked at a case where officers took a man's phone and simply pressed his own thumb to the sensor to unlock it.

lines.text: In 2024 the Ninth Circuit said pressing a thumb takes no thought at all. His body opened the door against him, and the Constitution had nothing to say about it.
source_lines: The court said that did not violate the Fifth Amendment. Pressing a thumb, they reasoned, takes no thought at all. His body opened the door against him — and the Constitution had nothing to say about it.

lines.text: But the court hinted the answer might have been different if the officers had made the man choose which finger to use.
source_lines: The court hinted the answer might have been different if the officers had made the man choose which finger to use

lines.text: Because choosing is a decision, and a decision happens in your mind. Same thumb. No protection if they press it. Maybe protected if you decide.
source_lines: because choosing is a decision, and a decision happens in your mind
A thumb they press to the sensor: no protection. The very same thumb, if you are the one who decides to use it: maybe protected.

lines.text: The courts' picture is a safe. They can force you to hand over the key, but not to tell them the combination.
source_lines: They can force you to hand over the key.
But they cannot force you to tell them the combination — because the combination lives in your mind, and speaking it is testimony.

lines.text: A passcode is a combination, a string of numbers that exists nowhere but inside your memory. A thumb is not.
source_lines: A passcode is a combination.
It's a string of numbers that exists nowhere but inside your memory.

lines.text: In 2025 the D.C. Circuit ruled the opposite: obeying that command admits the phone is yours, and that you know how to open it.
source_lines: In 2025, the D.C. Circuit ruled that forcing a man to unlock his phone with his fingerprint did violate the Fifth Amendment — because obeying that command, the court said, quietly admits something you know: that it's your phone, and that you know how to open it.

lines.text: So what protects you is not the lock on the phone. It is whether the choice to open it was ever yours.
